title: Chorus mini-dashboard: per-model & per-route compact performance spec
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Overview:
Design a compact, scannable mini-dashboard ("Chorus") that surfaces per-model and per-route performance signals for the Redwood Console. Chorus cards are intended for placement in route and model lists and the route detail header to allow quick triage without opening full charts. They should provide single-line summaries for latency p50/p95, throughput (requests/min), tokens per request, and a small sparkline of token volume.

Goals:
- Give engineers and SREs immediate, actionable signals in dense views (routes table, model catalog, project overview).
- Maintain parity with the primary performance canvas in terms of signal definitions so teams can rely on the mini view for initial triage.
- Keep visual noise low: compact typography, micro sparklines, color semantics for alerts, and an affordance to open the full inspector.

Target users:
- Platform engineers triaging model regressions
- Product engineers monitoring per-route SLA regressions
- On-call SREs needing a quick snapshot in an incident

Scope / Deliverables:
- Visual specs for the Chorus card in three sizes: tiny (table cell), small (route header), and medium (model list).
- Chart specs for the embedded sparkline and latency band thumbnail (p50/p95 ribbon).
- Content rules and fallbacks for stale data and low-sample routes.
- Interaction patterns: click -> full route model panel, hover tooltips, and quick mute/acknowledge action.
- Accessibility: color contrast targets and screen-reader label text for token counts and latency metrics.
acceptance_criteria: Chorus tiny (40px height) fits in routes table cell and shows: model short name, p95 latency (ms), token-per-request avg, tiny 36px sparkline, and an error badge if error_rate > 1%.

Chorus small (80px height) used in route header shows p50/p95 stacked numeric, throughput (rps), 72px sparkline with selectable 5m/1h/24h windows, and an expand control that opens the full performance canvas.
Latency band thumbnail renders p50 as line and p95 as semi-transparent band; all values use the same aggregation windows as the main console (5m/1h/24h).
All cards include an explicit 'no-data' state that suggests next steps (increase sampling or check model warm pools).
Design tokens, color names, and component anatomy documented in the Figma file and handed off to frontend with CSS variables and an accessibility checklist.
Prototype flows validated in a 30-minute design review with PM and 2 frontend engineers with recorded notes and at least one iteration addressing performance-of-render trade-offs.
decisions: Use numeric compact label for p95 with a micro-icon indicating percentile (e.g., 'p95') to avoid confusion with averages.
Sparklines will be SVG-based with simplified path generation to limit rendering cost in long tables; fallback to canvas for very large lists handled by engineering.
Color semantics: green=within-slo, amber=near-slo (75-100%), red=breach (>100% of configured SLO). These map to runtime thresholds exposed via the API.
Interactivity: clicking the card opens route detail (single-click) and a ctrl/cmd-click opens full performance canvas in a new tab to support on-call workflows.
tradeoffs: We deliberately favor compactness over exhaustive metrics. The mini-card will not show error breakdowns or per-model quantization details — those remain in the full canvas. This keeps the card consistent across list views at the cost of deeper context requiring an extra click.

notes_for_engineering:
- API expectations: card consumes compact telemetry endpoint that returns p50/p95, tokens_per_request_avg, requests_per_minute, error_rate, and a minified timeseries for the selected window.
- Provide a flag to opt-in to a high-fidelity timeseries for the medium card, but default to summary to avoid overfetching.
- Frontend should virtualize long lists and lazy-render sparklines.
- Provide unit test IDs for no-data and stale-data states.
